title: What Is My Public IP? Your Address, Explained
description: Find your public IP address using the lookup button, and learn what its approximate network location can and cannot tell you.
summary_sentence: For example, the address shown is the one every website you visit already sees — which is why checking it with a VPN on and off is the quickest privacy sanity check there is.
quick_answer: Choose Detect my public IP to ask the lookup provider which public address your connection uses for that request. The result can include approximate network and location details; it does not identify a precise physical address.
steps_intro: Use the detection button to check the address seen by the lookup provider:

body.t: Compare the reported address with your VPN enabled and disabled. A difference can be useful context, but an IP lookup alone cannot prove that all traffic or DNS requests use the VPN. For a specific address, use the
Whitelisting your home or office connection for a server starts with this number — and the knowledge that it may change when your ISP reassigns it.
“What IP are you coming from?” is support's way of finding your session in their logs. This page is the answer, ready to read aloud.
Offices, schools and carrier networks put many people behind one public address (NAT) — the page showing the same number on every desk is the architecture working, not a fault.

examples.label: Example · On and off the VPN

body.t: Run the lookup once with the VPN enabled and again with it disabled. Compare the reported addresses and network information. This checks only the connection to the lookup provider; it is not a complete VPN leak test.

examples.label: Example · The number changes — whose fault?

body.t: Most home connections hold dynamic addresses that rotate on reconnects or lease cycles. Yesterday's address being different is your ISP's normal housekeeping, not an intruder — security alerts live elsewhere.

faq: Is my public IP the same as my device's IP?

No — your device usually holds a private address (192.168…) inside your network; the router translates it to the one public address this page shows. The distinction is NAT, and it is why the whole street can share one public number.
Can someone find my home from this address?
Not from the address alone: public data resolves it to a network and an approximate area. Precise subscriber details sit with the ISP, released under legal process — the honest boundary, again.
Why does the page show IPv6 sometimes?
If your connection supports IPv4 and IPv6, the address shown depends on the connection used to reach the lookup provider. A single result does not test both address families.
My IP says a different city than mine.
Carrier and ISP routing centres concentrate addresses in hub cities. The shown geography is your network's, and for mobile connections it can sit a state away without anything being wrong.

A VPN shifts what sites see to the VPN's exit — a legitimate privacy tool with real trade-offs (speed, trust moved to the provider). This page is the measuring instrument either way: it shows what the world sees, so you can verify the choice works.
What is a static IP, and do I need one?
A fixed address that never rotates — sold by ISPs for servers and remote access. Most households neither have nor need one; dynamic addresses changing is normal, documented above.
Does the address reveal my browsing?
No — the address identifies a connection point, not activity. What you did on a site is that site's logs' business; the IP is merely the return address on the envelope.
IP addresses can change for several reasons, including switching networks, VPN routes, or ISP reassignment. A change alone does not establish whether a VPN is leaking.
